messages.subject: Memory retention model (Lee & Wagenmakers, 2014) issue
parts:
Hi Stan,

I'm trying to translate one of the models from Bayesian Cognitive Modeling book to Stan. Unfortunately, the part of the book from which is this model is not publicly available. But the problem is simple so I'll try to explain it.  

We have 4 subjects on memory experiment. They are given 18 words to remember. After that subjects are tested at 10 time intervals (as you can see in table below). All data for this model is in the table. Dashes stands for missing values. The model assumes that the probability an item will be remembered after a period of time t has elapsed is theta = exp (− alpha*t)+beta, with restriction theta <=1 .Graphical model is below. k[i,j] is data matrix, n is number of words to remember (=18), t[j] is length of time interval. 


Jags model and Stan translation is here https://github.com/neekro/Stan_translate/tree/master . My solution for missing values was to just exclude last row and last line from the data.


Stan model works fine for all subjects except subject 1. Here are all estimated parameters wrong. You can see it plots below (left on is from Stan, on right is from the book). Black line is actual data and white boxes are posterior predictive samples. It must be caused by the nature of Subject 1's data, but I didn't find out how to prevent it. 




























Thank you for any suggestions.

Cheers,
Martin

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Memory retention model (Lee & Wagenmakers, 2014) issue
parts:
Thanks for sending the detailed reports and working code.

As far as I can tell, the Stan program is a faithful translation
of the log probability function defined by the model.

I'm running the example now and it's super slow, both in
terms of iteration time and number of effective samples per
iteration. And if you do this:

head(get_sampler_params(samples,inc_warmup=FALSE)[[1]],n=100)

you'll see that n_divergent=1 for every iteration, which is
signalling a problem with the log probability during sampling (you
want n_divergent=0 for every iteration).

The problem is in the posterior.

Non-differentiable "link" functions are bad news, particularly
in Stan, which relies on derivatives. The link here for the
binomial parameter theta[i,j] is

theta[i, j] <- fmin(1.0, exp(-alpha[i] * t[j]) + beta[i]);

If alpha[i], beta[i] and t[j] are such that you get the 1.0
branch of fmin(), you lose all connection to the parameters in the model in
the neighborhood of the parameter values. For Stan this is bad because
without gradients, it devolves to a random walk.

What were the JAGS fits for the model in terms of alpha and beta?

I'd have tried to formulate this model using a differentiable link
function rather than f(u) = fmin(1,u). inv_logit is a typical choice,
which would set

theta[i, j] <- inv_logit(exp(-alpha[i] * t[j]) + beta[i]);

It's not a pure exponential decay, though.

Then you could also leave alpha and beta unconstrained --- I don't
understand why they're fixed in the current approach anyway, other than
to keep them near a range where the expression doesn't exceed 1.

Another thing you could do would be to put a constraint on beta
that kept it below max(exp(-alpha[i] * t)). The problem is that we can't declare
varying constraints, so it'd have to be done in a loop including the transform
and Jacobian. We're going to add in the constraint functions in the future
with built-in Jacobians, at which point this'll get easier.

It might also be convenient to declare theta as matrix[ns - 1, nt - 1] and
alpha and beta as vector[ns - 1].

You don't need to write alpha ~ beta(1,1) --- it's uniform and the default
with no sampling statement provided. It doesn't hurt to add it --- it just
incurs a couple of runtime checks that values are valid each time the log
prob is evaluated and adds a bit of extra overhead to autodiff.

I wrote a simple model and simulator, and Stan has a hard time fitting
with simulated data and the times given --- it's not much data, and I
don't know what the true posterior is --- the posterior intervals are very
wide, so it's getting the parameters in the posterior intervals at least.

Data simulated from the model doesn't look much like the real data.
This is highly subjective, but the real data asymptotes down to 4 at
different rates for all subjects. I think it'd be odd to get all those
4s from a binomial model with decay given the width of the intervals
and the exponential model.

- Bob
